role_context: At the advanced level, a Java Spring Boot engineer with 6+ years of experience is expected to independently design, implement, and maintain production-grade Spring Boot services, owning complex features across API design, service logic, persistence, security, integrations, configuration, and deployment readiness. They should make sound technical decisions around dependency injection, transaction boundaries, JPA performance, REST and messaging contracts, resilience patterns, observability, testing strategy, and runtime configuration with limited guidance, escalating mainly for broader architectural alignment or business-critical trade-offs. Day to day, they are expected to diagnose difficult framework, performance, data consistency, and production issues; refactor poorly structured services; manage upgrades and dependency conflicts; and ensure services meet standards for reliability, security, scalability, and maintainability. They also review Spring Boot code for subtle risks such as proxy limitations, transactional misuse, bean lifecycle problems, inefficient queries, insecure configuration, and weak test coverage, while guiding less experienced developers on practical Spring patterns and operational consequences.
questions_prompt:
Please ensure the questions you ask cover the key functional, logical, architectural, implementation, debugging, optimization, review, and problem-solving areas from the competency scope for {name}, matched to {proficiency} proficiency ({yoe} years experience).

Focus the assessment on applied Java - Spring Boot work items that require candidates to solve, fix, build, review, or reason through realistic engineering scenarios. Do not create trivia, syntax-only, semantics-only, installation/setup, test-framework, or configuration-lookup questions.

This is a basic proficiency, so the tasks need to match one year of experience only. Somebody with one year of experience does not have extensive production experience and their concepts are usually shaky, so the complexity of the task needs to be basic only. Let the candidate be able to finish this within 15 minutes.

Cover the following extracted competency areas and sub-skills explicitly through practical scenarios:

Core Java and Spring fundamentals:
- Object-oriented design principles as applied in Spring Boot services: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and composition.
- Interfaces, abstract classes, inner classes, and anonymous classes where relevant to service design.
- Generics, collections, streams, functional interfaces, lambda expressions, and method references in service-layer or data-processing logic.
- Exception hierarchy, checked vs unchecked exceptions, custom exceptions, and exception propagation.
- Concurrency concepts relevant to Spring services, including threads, locks, synchronized blocks, ExecutorService, and CompletableFuture in async workflows.
- Immutability, value objects, and correct equals/hashCode/toString behavior.
- SOLID principles and clean code practices for controllers, services, repositories, and configuration classes.
- Java memory model concepts in long-running Spring Boot services, including heap vs stack, garbage collection impact, object lifecycle, and memory leaks from static references or caches.
- Reasoning about dependency conflicts or version alignment only when they affect runtime behavior or Spring Boot autoconfiguration outcomes.
- Understanding how Java versions affect Spring Boot behavior, supported runtime choices, and production JVM implications.
- Reading and reasoning about JDK or external API documentation to integrate libraries cleanly.

Spring Core and dependency injection:
- Bean lifecycle: instantiation, dependency injection, initialization, and destruction.
- Bean scopes including singleton, prototype, request, session, application, and custom scopes, and when each is appropriate.
- Bean post-processors, BeanFactoryPostProcessor, BeanPostProcessor, and their behavioral impact.
- Circular dependency root causes, detection, and resolution strategies.
- Constructor injection as the primary dependency injection pattern, including trade-offs versus field and setter injection.
- Optional dependencies and lazy initialization decisions.
- Recognizing and refactoring over-wired classes and God-services.
- Java-based configuration using configuration classes, bean methods, imports, and profiles as design mechanisms rather than syntax recall.
- Conditional configuration and profile-based/environment-specific wiring.
- Component scanning boundaries, base packages, include/exclude effects, startup structure, ambiguous beans, name clashes, and unintended scanning.
- Spring Boot autoconfiguration behavior, cleanly overriding autoconfigured beans, enabling/disabling behavior, and internal starter design considerations.
- Spring proxying mechanisms, including JDK dynamic proxies vs CGLIB, AOP impact, transactional method behavior, self-invocation limitations, and restructuring code when proxies do not apply.

Spring Boot core concepts and application lifecycle:
- End-to-end application lifecycle: startup sequence, classpath scanning, environment preparation, context creation, autoconfiguration, and runners.
- Shutdown hooks, graceful shutdown, and lifecycle callbacks.
- Structuring applications for maintainability using packages, modules, feature-based organization, modular monoliths, or service extraction when appropriate.
- Application configuration management: properties vs YAML, property binding, externalized configuration sources, property source hierarchy and precedence, complex type binding, and configuration validation.
- Customizing Spring Boot behavior around logging, application environment, embedded server behavior, SpringApplication, profiles, profile groups, and profile-specific beans/properties.
- Effective starter usage, avoiding unnecessary starters, and considering bloat, startup time, and attack surface.
- Planning Spring Boot version upgrades, handling deprecations and behavior changes.

REST APIs, web layer, and reactive programming:
- Designing Spring MVC controllers with clear controller/service/repository separation.
- Handling path variables, query parameters, headers, cookies, matrix variables where appropriate, content negotiation, API versioning, and error handling conventions.
- Consistent error and exception handling using global exception handling patterns and appropriate HTTP status mapping for validation, business, and infrastructure failures.
- Serialization and JSON processing concerns including nulls, dates, time zones, enums, polymorphism, custom serialization, lazy JPA relations, bidirectional references, and large object graphs.
- Request/response validation, DTO boundary design, and mapping DTOs to domain models cleanly.
- Choosing between servlet and reactive stacks, including trade-offs between Spring MVC and WebFlux, and when reactive programming is beneficial.
- Basic working use of Mono/Flux, backpressure concepts, and integration constraints for reactive repositories or legacy systems.
- Cross-cutting web concerns such as filters, interceptors, argument resolvers, CORS, and rate-limiting strategies.

Data persistence and transaction management:
- Spring Data JPA entity mapping, relationships, cascade types, fetch types, and inheritance strategies.
- Repository design using CRUD, query methods, custom queries, and custom repository implementations.
- FetchType.EAGER vs LAZY implications, N+1 query problems, and mitigation strategies.
- Pagination and sorting in repositories and API exposure.
- ORM and JPA behavior: entity lifecycle states, persistence context, first-level cache, transactions, dirty checking, flushing behavior, and performance impact.
- Batch updates/inserts, statement caching, and JDBC-level optimization considerations.
- Transactional boundary design using propagation, isolation, readOnly, nested transactions, rollback behavior, checked/unchecked exceptions, private methods, self-invocation, and proxy pitfalls.
- Multiple data sources, multiple transaction managers, repository routing, and cross-database transaction feasibility.
- Alternative persistence choices such as Spring Data JDBC, MongoDB, Redis, NoSQL stores, message stores, criteria queries, query methods, and specification pattern.
- Schema and data model design, migration/versioning/rollback strategy, and alignment with domain concepts.
- Data integrity and consistency using optimistic/pessimistic locking, stale update handling, concurrency conflicts, and idempotent writes.

Security with Spring Security:
- Security filter chain behavior and Spring Boot security autoconfiguration impact.
- Authentication, authorization, and custom access decision logic.
- Username/password with persistent user stores, JWT validation, and OAuth2/OIDC client/resource server behavior at implementation level.
- URL-based vs method-level authorization, roles vs authorities, and mapping business permissions.
- Securing REST APIs with CSRF considerations for stateless APIs, CORS, secure headers, scopes/claims/roles, and security context management.
- Custom UserDetailsService, AuthenticationProvider, AuthenticationEntryPoint, access denied handlers, login flows, and API error responses.
- Common vulnerabilities and mitigations: SQL/JSON/header injection, XSS, CSRF, clickjacking, open redirects, hardcoded secrets, token/credential handling, and input validation/sanitization.
- Secure-by-default practices including limiting Actuator exposure, protecting sensitive paths, HTTPS/HSTS/TLS considerations, and avoiding secrets in code/logs/artifacts.

Integration, messaging, and asynchronous processing:
- Consuming and producing external HTTP services with appropriate timeouts, connection pools, and error handling.
- Resilient remote calls with retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallbacks.
- Messaging integration using Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS, or similar abstractions.
- Producer/consumer design, listener concurrency, error handling, payloads, headers, routing keys/topics, extensibility, and backward compatibility.
- Async and scheduled tasks using async execution, task executors, thread pool choices, scheduling behavior, context propagation, idempotency, and error handling.
- Channel-based or binder-based integration models where appropriate.
- Eventual consistency patterns including outbox/inbox, message deduplication, and at-least-once/at-most-once delivery trade-offs.
- API and message contract management through payload structure and semantics.

Architecture, design, and microservices with Spring Boot:
- Layered architecture with controller, service, repository, and domain boundaries.
- Ports-and-adapters/hexagonal or clean architecture using Spring beans and configuration.
- Recognizing when to keep a monolith, refactor into a modular monolith, or split into microservices.
- Service decomposition, avoiding over-fragmentation, service boundaries, APIs, and data ownership.
- Cross-cutting concerns including security, logging, observability, configuration, and error handling.
- Practical Spring Cloud usage such as service discovery, external config, client-side load balancing, and fault tolerance as implementation concerns.
- Inter-service communication trade-offs: REST vs messaging vs gRPC, synchronous vs asynchronous communication, coupling, and resilience.
- DDD-inspired design, bounded contexts, aggregate roots, Spring module organization, and keeping domain logic out of controllers.
- Balancing standards and flexibility with base configurations, shared libraries, internal starters, and justified exceptions.
- Architectural trade-off reasoning including cost/benefit of new Spring modules or third-party frameworks and operational impact on observability, deployments, and performance.

Performance, scalability, and reliability:
- Diagnosing slow endpoints, heavy queries, memory usage patterns, bottlenecks, and errors using profiling, metrics, logs, traces, and APM-style evidence.
- Throughput and latency optimization via web server thread pools, async executors, schedulers, database connections, timeouts, pool sizes, max connections, keep-alive, and compression.
- Common Spring/JPA performance pitfalls: N+1 queries, eager fetching, cascade misuse, inefficient serialization, excessive object creation, and large payloads.
- Scalability design with stateless services, external session state, workload partitioning, backpressure strategies, reactive designs, and messaging-based designs.
- Reliability patterns including retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, fallbacks, bulkheads, rate limiting, graceful degradation, and protecting critical resources.
- Resource management including JVM memory settings, GC behavior, and implications for long-running services.
- Interpreting performance/load/stress/soak results to guide code or configuration changes.

Observability, monitoring, and Actuator:
- Effective Actuator usage for health, metrics, info, environment, and custom endpoints.
- Securing and limiting sensitive operational endpoints.
- Meaningful health, liveness, and readiness information, including custom dependency health indicators for databases, messaging, and external APIs.
- Metrics and tracing with Micrometer-style custom business/technical metrics and distributed tracing concepts.
- Structured logging, JSON logs, correlation IDs, MDC, log levels, and avoiding sensitive data in logs.
- Using observability data to identify bottlenecks and errors and feed improvements back into code, configuration, or architecture.

Cloud, deployment, and runtime environments:
- Packaging and running Spring Boot applications as executable JARs/WARs where relevant to runtime decisions.
- Containerization design considerations such as efficient images and layered jars.
- Environment-specific behavior using profiles, environment variables, external configuration, config servers, and secret stores.
- Deployment targets including application servers, standalone JVMs, Kubernetes, and cloud PaaS, with health checks, probes, startup hooks, and shutdown hooks.
- Cloud integrations with databases, caches, message brokers, and cloud-specific Spring libraries where appropriate.
- Runtime robustness through logging, monitoring, alerting hooks, rolling deployments, blue-green/canary releases, and secure secret management.
- Incident response using logs, metrics, and traces to triage, mitigate, and prevent recurrence.

Build, dependency, and environment management as applied to real project outcomes:
- Multi-module project design only where it affects architecture, dependency boundaries, or runtime behavior.
- Dependency management, BOM/version alignment, transitive dependency conflicts, and Spring Boot autoconfiguration implications.
- Dependency upgrades with minimal disruption and remediation of vulnerability or compatibility issues.
- CI/CD reliability considerations only as they relate to delivering Spring Boot applications safely.
- Static analysis, security scanning, dependency vulnerability remediation, and project standardization when tied to practical code quality and risk reduction.

Collaboration, code review, and technical leadership:
- Explaining and defending design decisions using Spring capabilities and constraints.
- Identifying risks and trade-offs in proposed solutions.
- Reviewing Spring Boot code for correctness, security, performance, readability, maintainability, architectural fit, and Spring-specific pitfalls.
- Catching transactional misuse, bean scope issues, proxy/self-invocation problems, configuration anti-patterns, and dependency injection design smells.
- Helping others debug Spring behavior and interpret framework-driven outcomes.
- Collaborating with architects, product owners, QA, and operations to evolve services and communicate constraints.
- Contributing to shared Spring Boot standards, base projects, shared modules, incident post-mortems, and actionable improvements.

Documentation, governance, and knowledge sharing:
- Documenting APIs, message contracts, configuration options, environment-specific behavior, architecture, and component interactions.
- Keeping documentation aligned with implementation after refactors.
- Capturing limitations, feature flags, migration notes, deprecation plans, upgrade plans, and standards for security, logging, and error handling.
- Supporting compliance and auditability using evidence from configuration, code, and runtime behavior.

Task design guidance:
- Prefer realistic scenarios that assess understanding of requirements and constraints, reasoning about ambiguous real-world situations, quality of technical decisions and tradeoff analysis, identifying root causes, risks, and edge cases, proposing or implementing pragmatic solutions, and reviewing or improving existing work.
- Make tasks practical and work-item oriented: ask candidates to implement a small feature, fix a bug, diagnose a failure, improve a design, review a pull request, explain a trade-off, or propose a safe remediation plan.
- Avoid questions whose primary difficulty is remembering annotations, exact property names, command-line flags, tool setup steps, or test framework details.
- Calibrate the scenario complexity, code size, ambiguity, and expected depth to {proficiency} proficiency and {yoe} years of experience.

The goal is to evaluate applied competence, practical problem-solving, implementation and review ability, sound technical judgment, and the candidate's ability to deliver realistic solutions within the expected time constraints for their proficiency level.
